system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2144-06-27 21:22:00 to 2144-06-28 19:10:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient, a male with a history of liver transplant, chronic kidney disease, and chronic diarrhea, was admitted for nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea following a home flood. He was found to have acute kidney injury due to hypovolemia and urinary retention. A catheter was placed, and IV fluids were given, leading to improvement in renal function by hospital day 2. His nausea persisted, but infectious workup was negative, and he gradually tolerated oral intake. Tube feeds were restarted and advanced. He refused a planned flexible sigmoidoscopy but was able to maintain nutrition. He passed a void trial and was discharged home with stable kidney function, instructions to resume tube feeds, and recommendations for urology and PCP follow-up, including electrolyte monitoring due to prolonged QT syndrome.
problems: Personal history of other malignant neoplasm of large intestine
Hypertensive chronic kidney disease with stage 1 through stage 4 chronic kidney disease, or unspecified chronic kidney disease

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___ from the medicine team. I understand you've been having some discomfort when urinating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. It’s been burning when I pee for a few days now. I came in because I’ve had these infections before and didn’t want it to get worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was very smart. You also mentioned you’ve been feeling generally well otherwise—no fever, chills, or back pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing like that. Just the burning. I’ve been eating fine, walking around. I even brought dinner with me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. We’ve reviewed your records from the outside hospital. Your urine culture came back positive for Group B Strep, which is a type of bacteria that can cause UTIs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Group B Strep? I thought that was something pregnant women get tested for.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're right—it's common in that setting, but it can also cause infections in others, especially with a history like yours. The good news is it's sensitive to several antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because you're allergic to penicillin and ciprofloxacin, we started you on IV linezolid tonight to make sure we cover the infection safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do have a lot of allergies. What about my other meds? I take a lot for pain and my stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed all your medications. You’re staying on your regular doses—mycophenolate, prednisone, gabapentin, oxycontin, and the others. We’re also continuing your diarrhea meds, like loperamide and opium tincture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your renal ultrasound back. It looks completely normal—no blockage, no swelling in the kidneys. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my kidneys? I’ve had kidney issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidneys appear structurally fine. Your creatinine is a bit elevated at 1.9, but that’s consistent with your known chronic kidney disease. No sign of acute injury this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back negative—no bacteria in the blood. That means the infection is likely just in the urinary tract and hasn’t spread.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very good. We’re switching you from IV linezolid to oral cephalexin. It’s effective against the bacteria and safer for you given your allergies. You’ll take it three times a day for 14 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Do I need to come back for more tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. After finishing the antibiotics, you’ll need a repeat urine culture to make sure the infection is fully cleared. We’ve sent the order to your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also recommend you follow up with urology. Given your history of recurrent UTIs, they may want to look into possible causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I saw them a while ago. I’ll give them a call.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs this morning are stable. You’re feeling well, and your vitals are normal. We’re comfortable discharging you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you develop fever, chills, back pain, or worsening urinary symptoms, please seek care right away. Also, make sure to finish all the antibiotics, even if you feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And keep taking my regular meds like before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. All your home medications continue as prescribed. We’ve updated your list and sent it to your pharmacy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with cephalexin, and we’ve scheduled outpatient labs for the urine test. The results will be sent to your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a male with a history of liver transplant, chronic kidney disease, recurrent UTIs, and chronic pain, was admitted for dysuria. He was found to have a Group B Streptococcus urinary tract infection based on an outside culture. He was started on IV linezolid and later transitioned to oral cephalexin given his allergies. Blood cultures were negative, and a renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis or structural abnormalities. He remained afebrile and hemodynamically stable throughout the admission. His home medications, including immunosuppressants and pain regimens, were continued. He was discharged home with a 14-day course of cephalexin, instructions to complete the antibiotics, and plans for a follow-up urine culture and urology evaluation to address recurrent infections.
